(p-292) Surat al-Anfal is Medinan according to al-Hasan, Ikrimah, Jabir and Ata'. Ibn Abbas said: except for seven verses, from His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿And [remember] when those who disbelieved plotted against you﴾ [al-Anfal: 30], to the end of the seven verses.

﴿They ask you about the spoils of war. Say, "The spoils are for Allah and the Messenger. So fear Allah, and amend that which is between you, and obey Allah and His Messenger, if you are believers."﴾

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿They ask you about the spoils of war. Say, "The spoils are for Allah and the Messenger."﴾ This address is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when his companions asked him about the spoils (anfal) on the day of Badr.

Regarding these "anfal" about which they asked him, there are five opinions. The first: they are the booty (ghana'im). This is the view of Ibn Abbas, Ikrimah, Qatadah and al-Dahhak.

The second: they are the expeditionary detachments (saraya) that go ahead of the army. This is the view of al-Hasan.

The third: the anfal are whatever escapes from the polytheists to the Muslims without fighting, of beasts or slaves. This is one of the two opinions of Ibn Abbas.

The fourth: the anfal are the one-fifth (khums) of the fay' and the booty which Allah, Exalted is He, assigned to the people of the khums. This is the view of Mujahid.

(p-293) The fifth: they are additional gifts which the imam gives to some of the army according to what he sees as good.

"He comes to the wronged one from him, the Nawfal, the Zufar."

So Nawfal is one who gives much, and Zufar is one who carries the anfal (gifts); from it a man was named Zufar.

The second opinion: nafl means an increase of good, and from it comes the voluntary prayer (salat al-nafila).

Labid ibn Rabi'ah said:

"Indeed, the piety of our Lord is the best nafl, and by the permission of Allah is my delay and my haste."

They differed regarding the occasion of revelation of this verse according to four opinions. The first: what Ibn Abbas narrated, saying: "When the day of Badr came, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: whoever does such-and-such, for him is such-and-such. This was said by Ikrimah, Mujahid and al-Suddi.

Undoubtedly, they belong to Allah together with the world and what is in it, and the Hereafter; and the Messenger places them in the places where Allah commanded him to place them. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

The difference between one who cries for help (al-mustaghith) and one who seeks assistance (al-musta'in) is that the one who cries for help is one whose power has been stripped away, while the one who seeks assistance is one who is weak in power.

The difference between *istijaba* (answering, responding) and *ijaba* (answering) is that *ijaba* is a response that is not preceded by refusal.

﴿Indeed, I will reinforce you with a thousand of the angels, following one another﴾. Regarding it there are three opinions. The first: with every angel there is another angel, and this is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, so the thousand becomes two thousand.

The poet said:

*When Orion (al-Jawza') followed the Pleiades (al-Thurayya),*
*I suspected the household of Fatima of the suspicions.*

So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ dozed until they all slept, and then Gabriel gave the Messenger of Allah ﷺ the good news of victory, and he informed Abu Bakr of it.

Regarding Allah's favour upon them through sleep on that night, there are two aspects. The first: He strengthened them through rest for fighting on the following day. The second: He granted them security by removing fear from their hearts, as it was said: Security induces sleep, and fear keeps awake.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿a security from Him﴾ means tranquility and the calm of the soul from fear. In it there are two views. The first: a security from the enemy. The second: a security from Allah, glorified and exalted is He.

﴿And He sends down upon you water from the sky to purify you by it﴾, because Allah, Exalted is He, sent down upon them rain water as an aid to them in three matters. The second, which is the most special of their circumstances in that place: the sand was made firm by the water, so that the Muslims could fight upon it. The third: what Allah, Exalted is He, described of the state of purification.

Regarding their being purified by it, there are two views. The first: from the whisperings of Satan, by which he had cast fear into their hearts; this was said by Zayd ibn Aslam. The second: from the minor and major impurities that had befallen them; this was said by the majority of scholars.

Ibn Ata said: He sent down upon them water by which He purified the outward parts of their bodies, and He sent down upon them mercy by which He cleansed the inner secrets of their hearts.

Allah, Exalted is He, singled it out with this attribute for two reasons. The first: it is the most special of His attributes. The second: it is the most constant of His attributes.

The first: his whisperings, that the polytheists had overcome them over the water; this was said by Ibn Abbas. The second: his scheming, which is his saying: "You have no power against these people"; this was said by Ibn Zayd.

﴿and to strengthen upon your hearts﴾ may have two meanings. The first: confidence in victory. The second: through their gaining control over the water.

﴿and to make firm thereby the feet﴾. Regarding this there are two statements. The first: by the patience that Allah, Exalted is He, poured out upon them, so that they would stand firm against their enemy; this was said by Abu Ubayda. The second: the packing of the sand by the rain, on which no foot could remain firm; this is the view of Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and al-Dahhak.

Regarding this there are two views. The first: He said this to the angels as an aid to them. The second: He said this to him so that they would thereby strengthen those who believed.

﴿So strike [them] upon the necks﴾. Regarding this there are five sayings. The first: strike the necks, and "upon" (fawq) is an additional particle in the speech; this was said by Ata' and al-Dahhak. Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 8, verses 15–16:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿O you who believe, when you meet those who disbelieve advancing (zahf), do not turn your backs to them﴾. Al-zahf is drawing near little by little.

﴿Do not turn your backs to them﴾ means by fleeing from them and turning away from them.

On this there are two opinions. The first: this is general, forbidding flight after meeting the enemy.

The second: it is specific. God, exalted is He, had made it obligatory at the beginning of Islam that every Muslim man stand against ten polytheists, and after the encounter it was not lawful for him to flee from them. This is by His saying: ﴿If there are among you twenty who are steadfast, they will overcome two hundred; and if there are among you a hundred, they will overcome a thousand of those who disbelieve, because they are a people who do not understand﴾ [al-Anfal: 65]. On this there are two aspects. The first: they do not know what God, exalted is He, has imposed on them of Islam. The second: they do not know what God, exalted is He, has imposed on them of fighting.

Then this was abrogated (naskh) for them after their number increased and their strength grew firm. God, exalted is He, made it obligatory on every man who encountered the polytheists in battle to stand against two men, after it had been obligatory for him to stand against ten, as a lightening and a concession. This is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Now God has lightened your burden, and He knows that among you there is weakness﴾ (p-303). It was recited with a ḍammah and with a fatḥah on the ḍād (ḍaʿf / ḍuʿf). Regarding the difference between the two readings there are two aspects. The first: they are two dialects with one meaning, as said by al-Farrāʾ. The second: their meanings differ.

Regarding their difference there are two aspects. The first: with the fatḥah it is weakness in wealth, and with the ḍammah it is weakness in conditions. The second: with the fatḥah it is weakness in intentions, and with the ḍammah it is weakness in bodies.

It is also said that the reverse of the two aspects applies to the two aspects.

Then He said: ﴿So if there are among you a hundred who are steadfast, they will overcome two hundred; and if there are among you a thousand, they will overcome two thousand, by God's permission. And God is with the steadfast﴾. On this there are two interpretations. The first: God is with those steadfast in fighting, by aiding them against their enemies. The second: God is with those steadfast in obedience, by accepting their deeds and multiplying their reward. Thus it became binding upon whoever meets his enemy among the polytheists in battle that he not flee while he has the strength to endure, until God carries out His command as He wills. As for fleeing when unable to endure: if he is fought by more than twice his number, it is permissible for him to turn his back to them in flight. If he is fought by a number equal to twice his own, it is forbidden for him to turn his back to them in flight, except in one of two cases: either he withdraws to fight, which means fleeing in order to pursue and retreating in order to return, for war is advance and retreat, flight and pursuit; or he retreats to join another company in order to fight alongside it, whether that company is near or far. This is evident in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever turns his back to them on that day, except one who withdraws to fight or one who retreats to join a company, has certainly incurred anger from God﴾. That is, he has come to the place that makes God's anger due upon him, derived from al-mubawwaʾ, which is the place.

The school of al-Shafiʿi, his companions, and those who agree with them hold that this is general, applying to every Muslim who meets an enemy, and this was also the view of ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAbbas.

It is reported from al-Hasan, Qatadah, and al-Dahhak that this is specific to the people of Badr, and this was the view of Abu Hanifa.

On this there are two aspects. The first: they do not know what God, exalted is He, has imposed on them of Islam. The second: they do not know what God, exalted is He, has imposed on them of fighting.

Then this was abrogated (naskh) for them after their number increased and their strength grew firm. God, exalted is He, made it obligatory on every man who encountered the polytheists in battle to stand against two men, after it had been obligatory for him to stand against ten, as a lightening and a concession. This is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Now God has lightened your burden, and He knows that among you there is weakness﴾ (p-303). It was recited with a ḍammah and with a fatḥah on the ḍād (ḍaʿf / ḍuʿf). Regarding the difference between the two readings there are two aspects. The first: they are two dialects with one meaning, as said by al-Farrāʾ. The second: their meanings differ.

Regarding their difference there are two aspects. The first: with the fatḥah it is weakness in wealth, and with the ḍammah it is weakness in conditions. The second: with the fatḥah it is weakness in intentions, and with the ḍammah it is weakness in bodies.

It is also said that the reverse of the two aspects applies to the two aspects.

Then He said: ﴿So if there are among you a hundred who are steadfast, they will overcome two hundred; and if there are among you a thousand, they will overcome two thousand, by God's permission. And God is with the steadfast﴾. On this there are two interpretations. The first: God is with those steadfast in fighting, by aiding them against their enemies. The second: God is with those steadfast in obedience, by accepting their deeds and multiplying their reward. Thus it became binding upon whoever meets his enemy among the polytheists in battle that he not flee while he has the strength to endure, until God carries out His command as He wills. As for fleeing when unable to endure: if he is fought by more than twice his number, it is permissible for him to turn his back to them in flight. If he is fought by a number equal to twice his own, it is forbidden for him to turn his back to them in flight, except in one of two cases: either he withdraws to fight, which means fleeing in order to pursue and retreating in order to return, for war is advance and retreat, flight and pursuit; or he retreats to join another company in order to fight alongside it, whether that company is near or far. This is evident in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever turns his back to them on that day, except one who withdraws to fight or one who retreats to join a company, has certainly incurred anger from God﴾. That is, he has come to the place that makes God's anger due upon him, derived from al-mubawwaʾ, which is the place.

The school of al-Shafiʿi, his companions, and those who agree with them hold that this is general, applying to every Muslim who meets an enemy, and this was also the view of ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAbbas.

It is reported from al-Hasan, Qatadah, and al-Dahhak that this is specific to the people of Badr, and this was the view of Abu Hanifa.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 8, verses 17–18:

His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿So you did not kill them, but it was Allah who killed them﴾ admits of two meanings. The first: "But it was Allah who killed them by driving them towards you until He enabled you to overcome them."

The second: "But it was Allah who killed them by His aid to you, when He cast terror into their hearts and victory into your hearts."

There is also a third meaning, stated by Ibn Bahr: "But it was Allah who killed them by means of the angels whom He sent to reinforce you."

It has also been said: "You did not kill them by your own strength and weapons, but it was Allah who killed them by forsaking them and by seizing their spears."

﴿And you did not throw when you threw, but it was Allah who threw﴾. On this there are four opinions. The first is what Ibn Abbas, Urwah and al-Suddi related: "The Prophet (ﷺ) took a handful of dust on the day of Badr, threw it at them, and said: 'May the faces be disfigured' (shahati al-wujuh), meaning, may they be made ugly." From this is the saying of al-Hutay'ah:

"I see for myself a face which Allah has disfigured in its form, so ugly is the face, and ugly is its bearer."

So Allah, exalted is He, cast the handful into their eyes until it occupied them with themselves, and Allah granted the Muslims victory over them. This is the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you did not throw when you threw, but it was Allah who threw.﴾

The second: its meaning is "And you did not gain victory when you threw, but it was Allah who granted you victory," as said by Abu Ubaydah.

The third: "And you did not throw their hearts with terror when you threw their faces with dust, but it was Allah who filled their hearts with terror."

The fourth opinion: that he meant that his companions threw with arrows, and their throwing hit the mark.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But it was Allah who threw﴾ means by what He sent of the wind that helped their arrows, until they were aimed straight and struck.

What is meant by "throwing" here is hitting the target, because the meaning of "throwing" is understood as hitting; if one does not hit, it is said "he threw and missed."

When it is said without qualification, "he has thrown," nothing is understood from it except hitting.

Do you not see the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"So he threw it into its ribs"

Thus the mention of throwing sufficed without describing it as hitting.

And Dhu al-Rummah said regarding the arrow:

"He threw and missed, while decrees are overpowering, and so it turned back, and woe and war were its constant companions."

His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿And that He might bestow upon the believers a fine favour from Him﴾. The people of the subtle insights (ashab al-khawatir) said: "The fine trial (al-bala' al-hasan) is that which brings you contentment with it and patience under it." The exegetes said: "The fine trial here is the blessing of victory and booty."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 8, verse 19:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿If you seek a victory, then there has certainly come to you the victory﴾. Regarding this there are two views.

One of them: "If you seek victory from Allah, then the victory (al-fath) is the triumph (al-nasr), so there has certainly come to you the bounty of Allah by our being victorious." This is related from Ibn al-Anbari.

The second: its meaning is, "If you seek victory from Allah, and al-fath is al-nasr, then there has certainly come to you the victory of Allah for us over you." Regarding this address there are two views.

One of them: it is an address to the polytheists, because they sought victory on the Day of Badr, saying, "O Allah, cut off the one who is most severed from the ties of kinship and most unjust to his companion, so give victory against him." So Allah the Exalted gave victory to His Prophet and the Muslims over them.

(p-306) Then He said: ﴿And if you cease, it is better for you﴾, because the seeking of victory was against them, not for them.

﴿And if you return, We will return﴾. Regarding this there are two meanings. One of them: "And if you return to this denial, We will return to this affirmation (of the truth)."

The second: "And if you return to this seeking of victory, We will return to this granting of victory."

The second view: it is an address to the believers, whom Allah the Exalted helped on the Day of Badr when they sought His help. ﴿And if you cease, it is better for you﴾, meaning from what you did regarding the captives and the spoils.

﴿And if you return, We will return﴾. Regarding this there are two meanings. One of them: "And if you return to greed, We will return to censure."

The second: "And if you return to the like of what you did regarding the captives and the spoils, We will return to rebuking you."(p-306)

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 8, verses 20–23:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿Indeed, the worst of living creatures in the sight of Allah are the deaf and the dumb who do not reason﴾. As for al-Dawabb (living creatures, beasts), it is a term for everything that crawls upon the earth of its animal kind, because of its crawling upon it by walking; and it was more specifically used for horses.

The intended meaning of "the worst of living creatures" is the disbelievers, because they are the worst of the animals that crawl upon the earth.

Then He said: ﴿the deaf﴾, because they do not hear admonition.

﴿The dumb﴾: al-Abkam is the created being who is mute. He described them as dumb only because they do not acknowledge Allah, Exalted is He, nor the necessary consequences of obeying Him.

﴿who do not reason﴾ may bear two meanings. One of them: they do not understand from Allah, Exalted is He, His command and His prohibition. The second: they do not take heed as the people of reason take heed.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: this verse was revealed concerning the Banu ʿAbd al-Dar.

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿And had Allah known any good in them﴾ may bear two meanings: (p-307) One of them: guidance. The second: receptiveness.

﴿He would have made them hear﴾. In this there are three interpretations. One of them: He would have made them hear the proofs and admonitions with a hearing of understanding and instruction; this was said by Ibn Jurayj and Ibn Zayd.

The second: He would have made them hear the speech of those who asked for the revival of their dead from Qusayy ibn Kilab and others, bearing witness to your prophethood; this was said by some of the later scholars.

The third: He would have made them hear the answer to everything they asked about; this was said by al-Zajjaj.

﴿And even if He had made them hear, they would have turned away while they were averse﴾ may bear two meanings: One of them: even if He had made them hear the proofs and admonitions, they would have turned away from attentive listening and understanding. The second: even if He had granted them what they demanded, they would have turned away from belief.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 8, verse 24:

His saying, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿O you who believe, respond to Allah and to the Messenger﴾, meaning: answer Allah and the Messenger. Ka'b ibn Sa'd al-Ghanawi said:

﴿Many a caller calls, "O one who answers to generosity," but when that time comes, no responder responds to him.﴾

The response to Allah, exalted is He, is obedience to His command. It has departed from this wording only because it stands opposite to the calling to it, so it became a response to it.

﴿When He calls you to what gives you life﴾. Concerning this there are seven opinions:

The first: when He calls you to faith. This was said by al-Suddi.

The second: when He calls you to the truth. This was said by Mujahid.

The third: when He calls you to what is in the Qur'an. This was said by Qatadah.

The fourth: when He calls you to war and the striving against the enemy. This was said by Ibn Ishaq.

(p-308) The fifth: when He calls you to what ensures the continuance of your life in the Hereafter. This was mentioned by Ali ibn Isa.

The sixth: when He calls you to what brings about the revival of your affairs in this world. This was said by al-Farra'.

The seventh: that it is on the general sense of the call in what He has commanded them.

Al-Ala' ibn Abd al-Rahman narrated from his father, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ passed by Ubayy while he was standing and praying, so he called out to him. He said: (O Ubayy!) So he hastened in his prayer, then came, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: (What prevented you, when I called you, from answering me?) He said: O Messenger of Allah, I was praying. He said: (Did you not find in what was revealed to me: ﴿Respond to Allah and to the Messenger when He calls you to what gives you life﴾?) He said: Yes, O Messenger of Allah, I will not do it again."

﴿And know that Allah comes between a man and his heart﴾. Concerning this, the interpreters have seven opinions:

The first: He comes between the disbeliever and faith, and between the believer and disbelief. This was said by Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak.

The second: He comes between a man and his intellect, so that he does not know what he is doing. This was said by Mujahid.

The third: He comes between a man and his heart, so that he cannot be capable of faith or disbelief except by His permission. This was said by al-Suddi.

The fourth: its meaning is that He is near to his heart, coming between it and anything of his secret or open affairs being hidden from Him, so He is nearer to him than the jugular vein. This is a severe warning. This was said by Qatadah.

The fifth: its meaning is that He separates a man from his heart by death, so that he cannot make up for what has passed. This was mentioned by Ali ibn Isa.

The sixth: He comes between a man and what he wishes in his heart of survival, long life, victory and triumph. This was related by Ibn al-Anbari.

(p-309) The seventh: He comes between a man and what He places in his heart of terror and fear, or strength and security, so the believer is made secure from his fear, and the disbeliever fears His punishment.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 8, verse 25:

His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿And beware of a trial which will not strike those who have done wrong among you exclusively﴾. There are four opinions concerning it. The first: it refers to evil (al-munkar), that Allah the Exalted commanded the believers not to allow it to persist among them, lest the punishment encompass them all. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: it is the trial through wealth and children, as the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, your wealth and your children are a trial﴾ [al-Anfal: 28]. This is the view of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud.

The third: that the trial here is the affliction by which a person is tested. This is the view of al-Hasan.

The fourth: that it was revealed concerning marriage without a guardian (wali). This is the view of Bishr ibn al-Harith.

And it is possible that a fifth meaning is intended: that it is the open manifestation of innovations (bida').

Regarding His saying, the Exalted: ﴿will not strike those who have done wrong among you exclusively﴾, there are two possibilities. The first: the trial will not strike those who have done wrong. The second: the punishment of the trial will not strike, so that it becomes a punishment for the people of sins and a test for the people of righteousness.

There is also a third possibility: that it is a supplication for the believer that a trial not befall him. This is the view of al-Akhfash.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 8, verse 26:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And remember when you were few and oppressed in the land﴾, he means by that their fewness when they were in Makkah and their humiliation through the oppression of Quraysh towards them.

In this statement there are two aspects: (p-310) The first: that Allah reminded them thereby of His blessings upon them.

The second: the informing of the truthfulness of His promise to them.

﴿You feared that the people would snatch you away﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions. The first: by "the people" he means the disbelievers of Quraysh; this was said by Ikrimah and Qatadah.

The second: Persia and Rome; this was said by Wahb ibn Munabbih.

Then he explained what He had bestowed upon them, so He said ﴿and He sheltered you﴾. In this there are two aspects. The first: that is, He made for you a refuge in which you dwell secure.

The second: He sheltered you through the migration to Madinah; this was said by al-Suddi.

﴿And He strengthened you with His help﴾, that is, He strengthened you with His help for you against your enemies on the Day of Badr.

﴿And provided you with good things﴾, meaning from the lawful, and in this there are two opinions. The first: what He established for you of goodness.

The second: what He permitted you of the spoils of war; this was said by al-Suddi.

Al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: this verse was revealed specifically concerning the Muhajirun after Badr.

The Almighty said: ﴿O you who believe, do not betray God and the Messenger﴾. On this there are two views. The first: do not betray God, glorified is He, and the Messenger, peace be upon him, as the hypocrites did in their treachery. This was said by al-Hasan and al-Suddi.

The second: do not betray God and the Messenger concerning what He has placed among your wealth for His servants.

It may also bear a third meaning: betraying God is disobeying His Messenger, and betraying the Messenger is disobeying his words.

﴿And betray not your trusts﴾. On this there are three interpretations. The first: concerning what you have taken from the spoils (ghanima), that you should not conceal it from being brought to the common spoils (maghnam).

The second: concerning what God has entrusted to His servants of the obligations (fara'id) and rulings (ahkam), that you should discharge them rightly and not betray them by abandoning them.

[p. 311] The third: it is general, concerning every trust, that it should be discharged and not betrayed.

﴿while you know﴾. On this there are two views. The first: while you know that it is a trust without any doubt.

The second: while you know the sin (ma'thama) involved in betrayal, unlike one who acts out of ignorance.

al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: "This verse was revealed concerning Abu Lubaba ibn Abd al-Mundhir. The Messenger of God, peace be upon him, sent him to Banu Qurayza so that they would submit to the judgment of Sa'd. They consulted him, and he had secured his children and his wealth with them. He advised them not to do so, and gestured with his hand to his throat, indicating slaughter. So God, exalted is He, revealed this verse," up to His words: ﴿And know that your wealth and your children are only a trial, and that with God is a great reward﴾. This may bear two interpretations. The first: that what is with God, exalted is He, of reward is better than wealth and children. The second: that the reward with God, exalted is He, for a good deed, for which He recompenses tenfold, is greater than the punishment for an evil deed, for which He recompenses only with its equivalent.

So God, exalted is He, revealed this verse," up to His words: ﴿And know that your wealth and your children are only a trial, and that with God is a great reward﴾. This may bear two interpretations. The first: that what is with God, exalted is He, of reward is better than wealth and children. The second: that the reward with God, exalted is He, for a good deed, for which He recompenses tenfold, is greater than the punishment for an evil deed, for which He recompenses only with its equivalent.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 8, verse 29:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified, ﴿O you who believe, if you fear Allah, He will grant you a criterion (furqan)﴾. Regarding this there are four interpretations.

The first: the meaning of furqanan is guidance in your hearts by which you distinguish between truth (haqq) and falsehood (batil). This was said by Ibn Zayd and Ibn Ishaq.

The second: it means a way out (makhraj) in this world and the Hereafter. This was said by Mujahid.

The third: it means deliverance (najah). This was said by al-Suddi.

The fourth: it means victory and triumph (fath wa nasr). This was said by al-Farra'.

And it may admit a fifth: that He will separate between you and the disbeliever in the Hereafter.(p-312)

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 8, verse 30:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And [remember] when those who disbelieved plotted against you, to restrain you or kill you or expel you﴾. This was because the Quraysh conspired in the Dar al-Nadwa (the assembly house of Quraysh) against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). ʿAmr ibn Hishām said: "Bind him and imprison him in a house, and wait for him to meet the misfortunes of time (rayb al-manun)."

Abu al-Bakhtari said: "Expel him from among you on a driven camel, and you will be rid of him and of his harm to you."

Abu Jahl said: "This is not an opinion. Rather, kill him. Let a man from every tribe gather around him and let them strike him with their swords as one man strikes, and then the Banu Hashim will be satisfied with the blood-money (diyya)."

So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed this to His Prophet (ﷺ), and he went out to the cave with Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, and then migrated from it to Madinah. This was related by Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, and Qatada.

This is the explanation of His saying: ﴿And [remember] when those who disbelieved plotted against you, to restrain you﴾. Regarding it there are three opinions. The first: "to restrain you" means in chains; this was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, and Qatada.

The second: "to restrain you" means in imprisonment; this was said by ʿAta', ʿAbd Allah ibn Kathir, and al-Suddi.

The third: the meaning of yuthbitūka is yukhrijūka (expel you), as one says "qad uthbituhu fi al-harb" when you have driven him out in war; this was said by some of the later scholars.

Regarding ﴿or expel you﴾ there are two views. The first: "or expel you" from Makkah to some far corner of the earth, like exile (al-nafy).

The second: "or expel you" on a driven camel until you perish, or some of the Arabs seize you and kill you, thus relieving them of you; this was said by al-Farra'.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 8, verse 31–33:

(p-313) His saying, may He be exalted and majestic: ﴿And when Our verses are recited to them, they say, "We have heard. If we willed, we could say the like of this. This is not but the fables of the former peoples."﴾ This admits of two meanings. One: "We have heard this from you, and we will not obey you."

The second: "We have heard the like of this before, so what has it benefited you?"

﴿If we willed, we could say the like of this.﴾ This admits of two meanings. One: "The like of this in composition and eloquence, opposing it in its inimitability."

The second: "The like of this in argument, opposing it in its call to disbelief."

﴿This is not but the fables of the former peoples.﴾ That is, the tales of the former peoples. It admits of two meanings. One: that it is the stories of those who passed and the reports of those who came before.

The second: that it is taken from those who came before and is not a revelation from Allah, exalted is He.

It is said that this verse was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith ibn Kaladah. "The Prophet ﷺ had him killed in cold blood, along with three men from Quraysh: 'Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt, al-Mut'im ibn 'Adi, and al-Nadr ibn al-Harith. He was the captive of al-Miqdad. When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ ordered the killing of al-Nadr, al-Miqdad said, 'My captive, O Messenger of Allah!' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, '(O Allah, help al-Miqdad).' He said, 'This is what I wanted.'"

Concerning him Allah, exalted is He, revealed the verse that follows.

﴿And when they said, "O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky or bring us a painful punishment."﴾ In this statement there are two meanings. One: they said that out of obstinacy toward the truth and hatred for the Messenger ﷺ. The second: they said that out of belief that it was not the truth.

Concerning them was revealed the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿A seeker asked for a punishment that will occur﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 1]. Concerning them was also revealed the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿Our Lord, hasten to us our portion﴾ [Sad: 16]. 'Ata' said: "Indeed, some ten-odd verses of the Book of Allah, exalted is He, were revealed concerning al-Nadr."

His saying, may He be exalted and majestic: ﴿And Allah would not punish them while you are among them.﴾ This admits of two meanings. One: He said this to honor His Prophet and to exalt his rank, that He would not punish a people among whom he is present.

(Exalting his sanctity.)

(p-314) The second: His sending him among them is a mercy to them and a blessing upon them, so it was not permissible for Him to punish them while he was among them, until they deserved the removal of the blessing by his departure from them.

﴿And Allah would not punish them while they seek forgiveness.﴾ Regarding this there are five sayings. One: Allah would not punish the polytheists of Makkah while there remained among them Muslims who seek forgiveness. This is the saying of al-Dahhak, Abu Malik, and 'Atiyyah.

The second: He will not punish them in this world while they seek forgiveness in it, saying: "Ghufranaka" (Your forgiveness).

Ibn 'Abbas said: "The polytheists in Makkah used to circumambulate the House saying, 'Labbayka, labbayka, la sharika laka' (Here I am, here I am, You have no partner). The Prophet ﷺ would say, 'Enough, enough!' and they would say, 'Except a partner who is Yours, You own him and what he owns.' And they would say, 'Ghufranaka.' So Allah, exalted is He, revealed: ﴿And Allah would not punish them while they seek forgiveness.﴾" This was related by Abu Musa, Yazid ibn Ruman, and Muhammad ibn Qays.

The third: that seeking forgiveness in this context means Islam, and the meaning of the statement is: "Allah would not punish them while they submit (to Islam)." This was said by 'Ikrimah and Mujahid.

The fourth: "Allah would not punish one for whom entry into Islam has already been decreed by Allah." This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The fifth: its meaning is that if they sought forgiveness they would not be punished, as an invitation to them to seek forgiveness. This was said by Qatadah, al-Suddi, and Ibn Zayd.

The sixth: "Allah would not punish them," i.e., destroy them, while He knows that among them there are children and offspring who will believe and seek forgiveness.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 8, verses 34–35:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿Their prayer at the House was nothing but whistling and clapping.﴾ Regarding al-mukaʾ (whistling) there are two opinions. The first is that it is inserting their fingers into their mouths; this was said by Mujahid.

The second is that one interlaces his fingers, blows into his palm with his mouth, so that al-mukaʾ is the whistling (ṣafīr). From this is the saying of ʿAntarah:

"And the husband of Ghaniyyah, whom she left felled, his nostril whistling with the wind at the cheek of al-Aʿlam."

That is, it whistles with the wind when she stabbed him.

As for al-tasdiyah, there are five sayings. The first is that it is clapping (tasfiq), said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn ʿUmar, al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Suddi. From this is the saying of ʿAmr ibn al-Itnabah:

"They all remained, with them a din, a whistling (mukaʾ) by the House, accompanied by clapping (tasdiyah)."

The second is that it is obstructing (al-ṣadd) from the Sacred House; this was said by Saʿid ibn Jubayr and Ibn Zayd.

The third is that some of them confront others so that they do the same action, and whistle to him if he is distracted from it; this was said by some later scholars.

The fourth is that it is a form (taf ʿilah) from ṣadda yaṣuddu, which means clamor (al-ḍajīj); this was said by Abu ʿUbaydah.

From this is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿When your people turn away from it [in clamor]﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 57], meaning they clamor.

The fifth is that it is the echo (al-ṣadā) that answers the one who cries out, returning to him the like of his words; this was said by Ibn Bahr.

If it is said: Why did God, Exalted is He, call what they did at the House of whistling and clapping a prayer, when it was not one? (p-316) It is said that there are two answers to this. The first is that they would put clapping and whistling in place of supplication and glorification, so they made that a prayer, even though it was not a prayer in the ruling of the Sharia.

The second is that they would act in the manner of the actions of prayer.

﴿So taste the punishment because you used to disbelieve﴾. Regarding this there are two sayings. The first is the punishment of the sword on the Day of Badr; this was said by al-Hasan, al-Dahhak, Ibn Jurayj and Ibn Ishaq.

The second is that it will be said to them in the Hereafter, ﴿So taste the punishment﴾, and regarding this there are two aspects. The first: "then cast [yourselves into it]." The second: "then test it."

Muqatil related concerning the revelation of this verse that "when the Prophet ﷺ prayed in the Sacred Mosque, two men from the unbelievers of the Banu ʿAbd al-Dar ibn Qusayy stood, one on the right of the Prophet ﷺ whistling as the mukaʾ whistles, and the mukaʾ is a bird, and two men from them on his left clapping their hands, in order to confuse his prayer and his recitation, so this verse was revealed concerning them."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 8, verses 36–37:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve spend their wealth to avert [people] from the way of Allah﴾. There are two opinions concerning this:

The first: it is the expenditure of Quraysh in fighting the Messenger of Allah ﷺ on the Day of Badr. This was said by al-Dahhak.

The second: it is Abu Sufyan, who hired with his wealth on the Day of Uhud two thousand men from the Ahabish, and from them Kinanah (p-317), to fight the Messenger of Allah ﷺ with them, apart from those Arabs who joined him. This was said by Sa'id, Mujahid and al-Hakam ibn 'Uyaynah. Concerning this, Ka'b ibn Malik says:

We came to a wave of the sea, in its midst the Ahabish, some bareheaded and some helmeted.
Three thousand, while we were a small band; if we were many, three hundred, or four.

﴿So they will spend it; then it will become a source of regret for them﴾. This may bear two meanings:

The first: their spending of it will become a source of regret and grief for them.

The second: their disappointment in what they had hoped for, of victory over the Muslims, will become a source of regret that warns them afterward.

﴿Then they will be overcome﴾. He promised them victory and fulfilled His promise.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿so that Allah may distinguish the wicked from the good﴾. There are two meanings concerning this:

The first: the lawful from the unlawful.

The second: the wicked is that from which the rights of Allah, exalted is He, have not been paid, and the good is that from which the rights of Allah, exalted is He, have been paid.

It may bear a third meaning: the wicked is what is spent in acts of disobedience, and the good is what is spent in acts of obedience.

﴿and place the wicked one upon another﴾, i.e., He gathers it together in the Hereafter even if it was scattered in this world. ﴿and heap it all up﴾, i.e., He makes some of it upon others, and from this is His saying: ﴿then He piles it up as a heap﴾ [al-Nur: 43]. Concerning His saying: ﴿and puts it into Hell﴾, although wealth is not punished, there are two meanings:

The first: that He makes it a punishment in the Fire by which they are tormented, as He said: ﴿On the Day it will be heated in the fire of Hell﴾ [al-Tawbah: 35], and the verse continues.

The second: that He places their wealth with them in Hell, because they exalted themselves through it and gained strength in disobeying Allah; so He makes it with them in humiliation and punishment, just as it was for them in this world a source of honor and bounty.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 8, verses 38–40:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: If they desist, what has already passed will be forgiven them﴾ admits of two interpretations.

The first: If they desist from fighting and move to a truce (muwada'ah), He will forgive them what has already passed of seizure and punishment (al-mu'akhadhah wa al-mu'aqabah).

The second: If they desist from disbelief by embracing Islam, He will forgive them what has already passed of sins (al-athham).

﴿But if they return, then the way of the former peoples has already passed﴾. Its interpretation, according to the two former possibilities: According to the first interpretation, its meaning is: If they return to fighting, then the way (sunnah) of the former peoples has already passed concerning those who were killed and taken captive on the Day of Badr. This was said by al-Hasan, Mujahid and al-Suddi.

According to the second interpretation: the way of the former peoples from the earlier nations has already passed concerning what Allah seized them with in this world, of the punishment of annihilation (al-isti'sal).

Ibn 'Abbas said: "This verse was revealed concerning the people of Makkah after the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered it in the year of the Conquest, and he said to them: 'What do you think of me, and what do you think I will do with you?' They said: 'A noble cousin. If you pardon, that is what we expect of you, and if you take revenge, we have done wrong.' Then he (ﷺ) said: 'I say to you what Joseph said to his brothers: ﴿No reproach will be upon you today; may Allah forgive you, and He is the most merciful of the merciful﴾ [Yusuf: 92].' Then Allah revealed this verse."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 8, verse 41:

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And know that whatever you acquire as spoils of war, a fifth of it belongs to Allah, and to the Messenger, and to the near of kin, and the orphans, and the needy, and the wayfarer﴾. Allah, exalted is He, mentioned al-fay' (the property taken without fighting) in Surah al-Hashr and al-ghanima (spoils of war taken by force) in this surah.

The scholars differed concerning al-fay' and al-ghanima, in three opinions. The first: al-ghanima is what is taken from the property of the polytheists by force, and al-fay' is what is obtained from the land. This was said by 'Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib.

The second: al-ghanima is what is taken by force (ʿanwatan), and al-fay' is what is taken by a treaty (ṣulḥ). This was said by al-Shafi'i and Sufyan al-Thawri.

The third: al-fay' and al-ghanima are the same, and it is every property taken from the polytheists. The verse of al-fay' in Surah al-Hashr is abrogated (mansukha) by the verse of al-ghanima in Surah al-Anfal. This was said by Qatada.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿from anything﴾ means all that falls under the name of any lawful thing which the Muslims gain from the property of the polytheists.

﴿then indeed to Allah belongs a fifth of it﴾. One opinion: this is an opening of speech (istiftah kalam), for to Allah belongs this world and the next and what is in them; and the meaning of the speech is: indeed to the Messenger belongs its fifth. This was said by al-Hasan, 'Ata', Qatada, Ibrahim and al-Shafi'i. Nahshal related from al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent out a detachment and they gained spoils, he would divide the fifth of the spoils into five parts and spend that fifth on five [categories]." Then he recited: ﴿And know that whatever you acquire as spoils of war, a fifth of it belongs to Allah and to the Messenger﴾. The statement ﴿then indeed to Allah belongs a fifth of it﴾ is merely an opening of speech, since to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth; thus the share of Allah and the share of the Messenger became one.

The second: the share of Allah is due to His House, and its meaning is: indeed to the House of Allah belongs its fifth, and to the Messenger. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas related from Abu al-'Aliya al-Riyahi who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ would be brought the spoils, and he would divide them into five parts, four-fifths for those who witnessed them. Then he would take the fifth and put his hand into it, and take from it what his palm grasped, and set it aside for the Ka'ba, which is the share of Allah. Then he would divide what remained into five shares: one share for the Messenger, one share for the near of kin, one share for the orphans, one share for the needy, and one share for the wayfarer."

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿and to the Messenger﴾ has two opinions. The first: it is an opening of speech linked with the mention of Allah, and the Messenger has no share of it in that sense, just as Allah has no share of it in that sense; and the fifth is divided into four shares. This is the statement of Ibn 'Abbas through the narration of 'Ali ibn Abi Talha.

The second: that belongs to the Messenger, and this is the view of the majority.

The scholars differed concerning the share of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ after him, in five opinions. The first: it belongs to the caliph after him. This was said by Qatada.

The second: it belongs to the kinsfolk of the Prophet ﷺ by inheritance, and this is the view of those who held that the Prophet is inherited from.

The third: the share of the Messenger ﷺ is returned to the remaining shares, and the fifth is divided into four.

The fourth: it is spent on the general interests of the Muslims. This was said by al-Shafi'i.

The fifth: that it is spent on horses (al-kura') and weapons. It is related that this was the practice of Abu Bakr and 'Umar; narrated by al-Nakha'i.

As for His statement, exalted is He: ﴿and to the near of kin﴾, it has been differed upon in three opinions. The first: they are the Banu Hashim. This was said by Mujahid.

The second: they are all of Quraysh. Sa'id al-Maqri related: Najda wrote to 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas asking him about the near of kin, and he said: 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas wrote back to him: "We used to say that we are they, but our people refused this for us, and said: all of Quraysh are kin."

The third: they are the Banu Hashim and the Banu al-Muttalib. This was said by al-Shafi'i and al-Tabari.

The scholars differed concerning their share today, in four opinions: (p-320)
The first: it is for them forever, as it was for them before. This was said by al-Shafi'i.

The second: it is for the kinsfolk of the caliph who manages the affairs of the community.

The third: it is left to the Imam, who places it wherever he wishes.

The fourth: their share and the share of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ are returned to the remaining shares, which are three. This was said by Abu Hanifa.

As for ﴿the orphans﴾, they are those in whom four conditions are met. The first: the death of the father, even if the mother remains alive, because the orphanhood of human beings is by the death of fathers and not mothers, while the orphanhood of animals is by the death of mothers and not fathers.

The second: being young (al-sighar), according to the saying of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "There is no orphanhood after puberty (hulum)." The third: being Muslim, because it is the property of the Muslims.

The fourth: need, because it is prepared for the public interests.

Then concerning them there are two opinions: the first: it is for the orphans of the people of al-fay' specifically. The second: it is for all orphans.

As for ﴿the needy﴾, they are those who do not find what suffices them.

As for the wayfarers (ibn al-sabil), they are travellers among those in need, and being Muslim is taken into account for them.

Does it apply specifically to the people of al-fay'? Based on the two opinions.

Malik said: the fifth is held in suspension according to the opinion of the Imam regarding whomever he deems most deserving of it, and these categories were mentioned only because of the genuineness of their need at that time.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And what We sent down upon Our servant on the Day of al-Furqan, the day the two hosts met﴾. It is the Day of Badr, on which Allah, exalted is He, distinguished between truth and falsehood.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 8, verse 42:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿When you were on the nearer side of the valley﴾ means the edge of the valley at Badr, the side nearer to Madinah.

﴿And they were on the farther side﴾ means the farther edge of the valley, nearer to Makkah.

Al-Akhfash said: the ʿudwa (side, slope) of the valley is the slope of its edge, which is higher than its bottom and lower than its top.

﴿And the caravan was below you﴾ means the caravan of Abu Sufyan at the bottom of the valley. Al-Kalbi said: on the shore of the sea, three miles away.

﴿And even if you had made a mutual appointment, you would have differed concerning the appointment﴾. Concerning this there are three interpretations. The first: even if you had made an agreement to meet together, you would have differed about the appointment, through advancing, delaying, adding and reducing, without intending that.

The second: even if you had made an appointment and then the great number of your enemy and the smallness of your number had reached you, you would have held back and broken the appointment. This was said by Ibn Ishaq.

The third: even if you had made an appointment and then the great number of your enemy had reached you without God's help to you, you would have broken the appointment with obstacles and impediments.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿That he who perished might perish by clear evidence and he who lived might live by clear evidence﴾. Concerning this there are two interpretations. The first: that those of the polytheists of Quraysh who were killed at Badr would be killed after proof, and that whoever remained would remain by [God's] power.

The second: that whoever of Quraysh disbelieved after the proof, through the clarification of what they had been promised, would disbelieve, and whoever believed after knowledge of the soundness of their faith would believe.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 8, verses 43–44:

His saying, may He be exalted and majestic: ﴿When Allah showed them to you in your dream as few.﴾ There are two interpretations concerning this. The first: Allah showed His Prophet ﷺ the fewness of the polytheists with his own eyes (ʿayānan). His words ﴿in your dream﴾ mean in your eyes, which are the place of sleep. This was said by al-Hasan.

The second: He cast sleep upon him and showed him their fewness in his sleep. This is the apparent meaning, and it is the view of the majority (al-Jumhur).

Allah showed him this contrary to what it actually was, as a gentle favor bestowed upon him and upon his community, so that it would make their hearts more firm and make them more ready to meet their enemy. Had it not been for this, such a state would not have been permissible from Allah, the Exalted, concerning His Prophet ﷺ. ﴿And if He had shown them to you as many, you would have lost heart and disputed about the matter﴾. There are two interpretations concerning this. The first: you would have disagreed about meeting them or about holding back from them.

The second: you would have been cowardly toward them and fled from them.

﴿But Allah saved [you]﴾ admits of two interpretations. The first: He saved you from failure (fashal).

The second: you would have been cowardly toward them and fled from them, but Allah saved you from the enemy.

There is also a third: but Allah saved His command concerning them, until what He had decreed concerning their destruction was carried out.

The second: they came at them from their front and their back; whoever was in front of them struck their faces, and whoever was behind them struck their backs.

Allah the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿And if you fear treachery from a people﴾, meaning, in the breaking of the covenant.

﴿Then throw back to them [their treaty] on equal terms﴾, that is, cast their covenant back to them, so that they cannot attribute to you treachery toward them.

Al-nabdh (throwing away, rejecting) is al-ilqa' (casting down).

The poet said:

؎ "They cast forth from speech with which they hit the places of water, for the thirsty one who is parched."

Regarding His words, Exalted is He, ﴿on equal terms﴾, there are five aspects:

The first: on equal footing (ʿalā mahl, "with deliberation"). This was stated by al-Walid ibn Muslim.

The second: on the basis of withdrawal from what they do to you (ʿalā muḥājazah), as stated by Ibn Bahr.

The third: on equal footing in knowledge, so that they do not outpace you in doing what they intend against you.

The fourth: on justice without injustice (ʿalā ʿadl min ghayr ḥayf), and he cited the verse of the rajiz (rajaz poet):

؎ "Strike the faces of the perfidious and the enemies, until they answer you with equal terms."

That is, to justice.

The fifth: on the middle path (ʿalā al-wasaṭ), and its speaker cited the words of Ḥassān:

؎ "Woe to the helpers of the Prophet and his kin, after the setting, in the level of the grave-niche."

Mujahid mentioned that it was revealed concerning the Banu Qurayza.

The Exalted said: ﴿And prepare against them whatever you can of power and of steeds of war﴾. On this there are five opinions. The first is that "power" means male horses and "steeds of war" (ribāṭ al-khayl) means female horses; this is the view of ʿIkrima.

The second is that "power" means weapons; this was said by al-Kalbī.

The third is that "power" means mutual sincerity and unity of word.

The fourth is that "power" means trust in God, the Exalted, and turning to Him.

The fifth is that "power" means archery.

Yazīd ibn Abī Ḥabīb narrated from Abū ʿAlī al-Hamadhānī, from ʿUqba ibn ʿĀmir, who said: "I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say on the pulpit: ﴿And prepare against them whatever you can of power﴾. Indeed, power is archery," and he said it three times.

(p-330) ﴿And of steeds of war﴾: according to the view of ʿIkrima, this refers specifically to females, while according to the view of the majority (al-Jumhūr, the majority of scholars), it is general, covering both males and females.

ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ narrated that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Keep horses tethered, for their backs are a source of honour for you, and their bellies are a treasure for you."

﴿To strike terror thereby into the enemy of God and your enemy﴾. On this there are two opinions. The first: "the enemy of God" is the disbeliever, and "your enemy" is the one who opposes you. The second: "the enemy of God" is your enemy, because the enemy of God is an enemy to His allies.

Al-irhāb (striking terror) means intimidation.

﴿And others besides them, whom you do not know, but God knows them﴾. On this there are five opinions. The first: they are the Banū Qurayẓa; this was said by Mujāhid.

The second: they are the people of Persia and Rome; this was said by al-Suddī.

The third: they are the hypocrites; this was said by al-Ḥasan and Ibn Zayd.

The fourth: they are the devils; this was said by Muʿādh ibn Jabal.

The fifth: they are everyone whose enmity you do not recognise; this was said by some of the later scholars.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 8, verses 61–63:

His saying, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿And if they incline to peace, then incline to it﴾. In this there are three interpretations (wujūh). The first: "And if they lean toward truce (muwada'a), then you lean toward it."

(p-331) The second: "And if they hold back from war, seeking peace with you, then you hold back from them, seeking peace with them."

The third: "And if they show Islam, then accept from them the outward of their Islam, even if the inward of their belief differs."

In this there are three opinions (aqawil). The first: it is general concerning the truce with every polytheist (mushrik) who asks for it, and then it was abrogated (nuskhat, naskh) by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ [al-Tawba: 5]. This was said by al-Hasan, Qatada and Ibn Zayd.

The second: it concerns only the People of the Book (Ahl al-Kitab) when they offer the jizya (poll tax).

The third: it concerns specific people who asked for truce, and He commanded that their request be granted.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 8, verse 64–66:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿O Prophet, Allah is sufficient for you and for those believers who follow you﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations. The first: "Allah is sufficient for you, and sufficient for the believers who follow you," as said by al-Kalbi and Muqatil.

The second: "Allah is sufficient for you" means that you should put your trust in Him, and "the believers" means that you should fight with them.

Al-Kalbi said: This verse was revealed at al-Bayda', on the expedition of Badr, before the fighting.

(p-332) His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿O Prophet, urge the believers to fight. If there are twenty among you who are steadfast, they will overcome two hundred; and if there are a hundred among you, they will overcome a thousand﴾. That is, they will fight a thousand. Mujahid said: This was on the Day of Badr, when each man among the Muslims was made responsible for fighting ten of the polytheists, and that was hard for them, so it was abrogated by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Now Allah has lightened your burden﴾. Ibn Bahr said: its meaning is that Allah, Exalted is He, grants victory to each man among the Muslims over ten of the polytheists. The interpretation of these two verses has already passed earlier.

﴿It is not for a prophet to have captives until he has inflicted a massacre upon the land﴾. This was revealed concerning the captives of Badr, when the Prophet ﷺ settled, after consulting his companions, on ransoming them with wealth, each captive for four thousand dirhams. Allah rebuked him for this and said that it was not for him to ransom the captives.

﴿Until he has inflicted a massacre upon the land﴾: there are two interpretations. The first is that it means dominance and subjugation, as said by al-Suddi.

The second is that it means the great slaughter of the enemy, so that the Muslims are honoured by it and the polytheists are humiliated by it, as said by Mujahid.

﴿You desire the goods of this world﴾: this means wealth, which he called "goods" (ʿaraḍ) because of its brief duration.

﴿But Allah desires the Hereafter﴾: this means acting in a way that brings the reward of the Hereafter.

﴿Had there not been a decree from Allah that had preceded, a great punishment would have touched you for what you took﴾: this means the wealth you took as ransom for the captives of Badr.

Concerning His words ﴿Had there not been a decree from Allah that had preceded﴾ there are four opinions:

The first: Had there not been a decree from Allah that had preceded for the people of Badr that He would not punish them, a great punishment would have touched them for what they took as ransom for the captives of Badr. This was said by Mujahid and Saʿid ibn Jubayr.

The second: Had there not been a decree from Allah that had preceded, that He would make the spoils lawful for you, a great punishment would have touched the people of Badr for hastening to take them. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Abu Hurayra, al-Hasan, and ʿUbayda.

The third: Had there not been a decree from Allah that had preceded, that He would not hold anyone accountable for an action done in ignorance, a great punishment would have touched you for what you took. This was said by Ibn Ishaq.

The fourth: Had there not been a decree from Allah that had preceded, which is the Qur'an in which you believed, requiring the forgiveness of minor sins, a great punishment would have touched you for what you took.

«The Prophet ﷺ had consulted Abu Bakr and Umar concerning the captives of Badr. Abu Bakr said: "They are your people and your kin, so spare them, perhaps Allah will guide them." Umar said: "They are the enemies of Allah and the enemies of His Messenger; they denied you and expelled you, so strike their necks." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ then inclined, after turning away from them, to the opinion of Abu Bakr, and took the ransom of the captives so that the Muslims would be strengthened by it, and he said: "You are a burden in the eyes of the emigrants." Then, when this verse was revealed, the Prophet ﷺ said: "Had we been punished for this matter, O Umar, none would have been saved except you."»

Then Allah, the Exalted, made clear the permissibility of the spoils and the ransom with His words: ﴿So eat of what you have taken, lawful and good﴾.

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying: ﴿O Prophet, say to those prisoners who are in your hands: If Allah knows any good in your hearts, He will give you better than what was taken from you﴾ admits of two interpretations. The first: [it will give you] what is more lawful (aḥall) than what was taken from you.

The second: [it will give you] more than what was taken from you.

It was said: "This verse was revealed when al-cAbbas ibn cAbd al-Muttalib was taken prisoner along with the prisoners of Badr. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took from him the ransom for himself and for his two nephews, ʿAqil and Nawfal. He said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I was a Muslim, but I was brought out [to fight] under compulsion, and you have left me poor, begging from the people.'

He (ﷺ) said: 'Where is the wealth that you handed over to Umm al-Fadl when you departed?' [al-cAbbas] said: 'Allah has increased our certainty in your prophethood.'

Al-cAbbas said: 'Allah the Mighty and Majestic has fulfilled His promise to me regarding what He has given me. I have twenty slaves, and each slave trades with twenty thousand [dirhams], and Allah the Mighty and Majestic has given me better than what was taken from me on the day of Badr.'"

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, those who believed﴾, meaning: in Allah.

﴿And emigrated﴾, meaning: they emigrated and left their homes in obedience to Allah.

﴿And strove with their wealth and their lives in the cause of Allah﴾. Striving with wealth means spending, and striving with the self means fighting. These are the emigrants who went with the Prophet (ﷺ) to Madinah.

Then He said: ﴿And those who gave shelter and helped﴾, meaning the Ansar, who sheltered the emigrants in their homes and helped the Prophet (ﷺ) and helped them.

﴿They are allies of one another﴾. There are two interpretations of this. The first: they are helpers of one another. This is the view of the majority (al-Jumhur).

The second: they have a greater right to the inheritance of one another.

Ibn Abbas said: Allah the Exalted made inheritance for the emigrants and the Ansar, to the exclusion of the relatives by blood (dhawu al-arham).

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And those who believed but did not emigrate, you have no obligation of protection toward them at all until they emigrate﴾, meaning: you have no share of their inheritance at all until they emigrate. They knew this until Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿And blood relatives are closer to one another in the Book of Allah﴾, meaning in inheritance. Thus the earlier ruling was abrogated (naskh), and inheritance passed to blood relatives. This was said by Mujahid, Ikrimah, al-Hasan and al-Suddi.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 8, verse 73:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified, ﴿And those who disbelieve, some of them are allies of others﴾, has two interpretations. The first: some of them are helpers of others; this is the view of Qatadah and Ibn Ishaq.

The second: some of them are heirs of others; this is the view of Ibn Abbas and Abu Malik.

﴿Unless you do it, there will be fitnah (turmoil; trial) on earth﴾. Concerning this there are two explanations. The first: unless you lend support to one another, O believers, ﴿there will be fitnah on earth﴾, meaning through the dominance of the disbelievers.

﴿And great corruption﴾, through the weakening of faith; this is the view of Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Jarir.

The second: unless you inherit from one another through Islam and emigration (hijrah), ﴿there will be fitnah on earth﴾ through division of the word (ikhtilaf al-kalimah; disunity).

﴿And great corruption﴾, through strengthening the one who secedes from the community (al-jama'ah); this is the view of Ibn Abbas and Ibn Zayd. And Allah knows best.
